title: End of Life
description: End-of-life care simulation. Laura C. Anderson, a 35-year-old with end-stage metastatic lung cancer, arrives in the ED with decreased level of consciousness and respiratory difficulty. Students assess common end-of-life symptoms, communicate therapeutically with Laura and her mother about hospice and advance directives, and implement hospitalist admission orders.

learningObjectives.text: Communicate effectively and compassionately with the patient, family, and health care team members about end-of-life issues
Recognize one's own attitudes, feelings, values, and expectations about death and the individual, cultural, and spiritual diversity existing in these beliefs and customs
Demonstrate respect for the patient's views and wishes during end-of-life care

Assess symptoms (e.g., pain, dyspnea, constipation, anxiety, fatigue, nausea/vomiting, skin breakdown and altered cognition) commonly experienced by patients at the end of life and intervene appropriately according to evidence based palliative care practices
Apply legal and ethical principles in end-of-life care, recognizing the influence of personal values, professional codes, and patient preferences
Address spiritual health during end-of-life care

outcomes: Implement one's role as a nurse in ways that reflect integrity, responsibility, ethical practices, and an evolving professional identity as a nurse committed to evidence-based practice, caring, advocacy and quality care
Demonstrate appropriate written, verbal, and nonverbal communication in a variety of clinical contexts
Integrate social, mathematical, and physical sciences, pharmacology, and pathophysiology in clinical decision making
Provide patient centered care by utilizing the nursing process across diverse populations and health care settings
Minimize risk of harm to patients, members of the healthcare team and self through safe individual performance and participation in system effectiveness
Lead the multidisciplinary health care team to provide effective patient care throughout the lifespan
Use information and technology to communicate, manage data, mitigate error, and support decision-making
Maintain a safe, effective care environment for adults of all ages
Differentiate scopes of practice within the nursing profession
Provide nursing care for patients with comfort alterations
Provide nursing care for patients with nutritional, fluid, and electrolytes disturbances
Provide nursing care for patients with commonly occurring alterations in elimination patterns
Provide nursing care for patients and families experiencing grief and loss
Provide nursing care for patients with alterations in oxygenation
Provide nursing care for patients with sleep/rest/mobility alterations
Adapt nursing practice to meet the needs of diverse patients in a variety of settings
Provide nursing care for patients with integumentary disorders

historyAndPhysical.chiefComplaint: Decrease in level of consciousness and respiratory difficulty
historyAndPhysical.hpi: This is a 35-year-old female brought to the ER with decrease in level of consciousness and respiratory difficulty. She has end stage lung cancer. Biopsy of right lower lobe 9 months ago revealed carcinoma that has now metastasized to the bone and brain. The patient has received eight monthly cycles of chemotherapy but requested hospice services one week ago according to her oncologist, Dr. Benton. She is accompanied by her mother who states she wants "everything possible done for her daughter." No advance directives are in place.
historyAndPhysical.pastMedicalHistory: Lung Cancer with metastasis to brain and bone
medications: Fentanyl patch 25 mcg every 72 hours for pain
Oxycodone ER 80 mg PO every 12 hours PRN for pain
Docusate sodium 100 mg PO BID for constipation
Compazine 10mg PO every 4-6 hours for nausea PRN
historyAndPhysical.familyHistory: Single; no children; lives alone. Mother Jane Beckman is emergency contact. Father (Jane's husband) passed away.

reviewOfSystems.findings: Mother reports change in level of consciousness. Denies headaches or change in vision.
Complains of productive cough of white, blood streaked sputum and worsening shortness of breath. Complains of chest pain worse on inspiration.
Denies claudication, leg cramps, paresthesias or edema.

Mother reports "no appetite" and "has been losing a lot of weight." Patient complains of nausea and vomiting relieved with Compazine. Patient complains of constipation that she treats with docusate sodium.
Patient reports dark, concentrated urine but no dysuria or hematuria.

examVitals.O2Sat: 85% on RA (paramedics); 89% on O2 1L in room

physicalExam.findings: 35-year-old female who appears emaciated and withdrawn. Alert but drowsy. Avoided eye contact and stated, "Just let me die."
Eyes open to speech, oriented x3. Visibly fatigued. Flat affect. GCS 14.
Course crackles throughout with occasional wheeze.
Strength 2/5. Sensation and reflexes intact. Skin dry.

historyAndPhysical.assessmentAndPlan:
End stage cancer; end of life.
• Admit to medical floor for pain management.
• Initiate home medications.
• Hydromorphone IV 0.5mg STAT and every 2 hours PRN for severe pain.
• Dexamethasone 20 mg PO.
• Bedrest.
• Diet as tolerated.
• Oxygen therapy to maintain O2 sat >90%.
• Consult for respiratory therapy.
• Palliative care consult.

I discussed with patient and mother her current end-stage lung cancer status and recommended hospice care, initiation of advance directives and DNR status. No decision was made so will order follow-up with palliative care consult.

Laboratory and diagnostic studies: ABGs STAT, CBC, Chem 7.

orders.order: Maintain O2 sat > 90%, start O2 via NC at 2 L and titrate prn
Hydromorphone 0.5mg IV every 2 hours PRN for severe pain
Fentanyl patch 25 mcg every 72 hours for pain
Oxycodone ER 80 mg PO every 12 hours PRN for pain
Docusate sodium 100 mg PO BID for constipation
Compazine 10mg PO every 4-6 hours for nausea PRN

mar.order: Fentanyl patch 25 mcg every 72 hours for pain
Oxycodone ER 80 mg PO every 12 hours PRN for pain
Docusate sodium 100 mg PO BID for constipation
Compazine 10mg PO every 4-6 hours for nausea PRN
Hydromorphone 0.5mg IV every 2 hours prn for severe pain

states.title: Patient Assessment
states.patientOverview: Patient is drowsy and is in severe pain that is not being managed by current medication. She desires hospice and states "just want to stop hurting," but her mom still wants everything done. No advance directives are in place and patient is full code. End of life concerns include: pain, shortness of breath, anxiety/fear/depression, nausea, constipation, no appetite/weight loss, fever. Patient also has Stage 1 pressure ulcer on gluteus that has not yet been noticed.
expectedStudentBehaviors: Introduce themselves
Verify the patient (Scan QR Code: Patient ID)
Obtain vital signs
Students must enter vitals on the iPad, but the accuracy of those vitals are not tied to iPad programming
Assess chief complaint: pain
Assess respiratory status and relate to patient condition
Titrate oxygen therapy
Perform a thorough skin assessment (Scan QR Code: Sacral)
Recognize Stage 1 pressure ulcer on gluteus and implement appropriate interventions for an end of life patient
Assess GI status: hypoactive bowel sounds, nausea, lack of appetite
Communicate therapeutically with mom and patient about end of life issues such as hospice and pain control; DNR; and advance directives
May watch patient education video about advance directives with the patient and/or mom
May assist patient to complete the advance directive form located in Appendix A
Call provider to advocate for pain medications
May address spiritual health and call a chaplain or pastor

technicianPrompts.response: Patient is drowsy with flat, withdrawn affect.
"Just let me sleep."
"It hurts so bad, nothing helps."
"I just want to stop hurting."

technicianPrompts.trigger: if students assist with advanced directive form
technicianPrompts.response: Use the completed copy (Appendix B) as prompts for answering the questions.
"She still has a lot of life to live. I want everything done for her."
"I found her lying on the floor this morning. She barely recognized me."
"I am the emergency contact for Laura."
"My husband passed away. It's just Laura and me now."
"She uses a Fentanyl patch and oxycodone for pain."
"We don't need advanced directives. Do everything you can!"

facilitatorQuestions: What are your concerns based on your pain assessment findings?
What risk factors does Laura have for skin breakdown? How would you describe the skin changes on her gluteus? What interventions should be implemented?
What are some possible causes for Laura's constipation?
What are some possible causes for Laura's nausea and lack of appetite?
What stage of grief do you think Laura is experiencing today?
What stage of grief do you think Jane (her mom) is experiencing today?
What is hospice care? How would it benefit Laura and Jane?
What are advance directives? How would they benefit Laura?
How can spirituality be addressed with Laura and Jane?
What is Laura's fluid and nutritional status? Are any interventions required at this time?

states.title: New Orders from the Hospitalist
states.patientOverview: The student receives a message that reads, "New orders have been received." The student(s) should review and implement the new admission orders. The patient continues to be drowsy and in pain. The patient wants to stop treatment for cancer and go home to die peacefully. The mother continues to want everything done for Laura.
expectedStudentBehaviors: Prioritize implementation of new orders
Call RT for consult
Call palliative care for consult
Titrate oxygen PRN
Call lab for lab work
Determine what medications should be administered at this time

technicianPrompts.response: "How is hydromorphone going to help me?"
"How is hydromorphone different from the oxycodone and Fentanyl that I'm already on?"
"Are there any side effects from the hydromorphone?"
"How will the Dexamethasone help me?"
"I just want to stop hurting."
Patient refuses lab work and ABGs stating, "I don't want anyone else poking me."
"I feel queasy."
"I feel bloated."
"I haven't been able to go to the bathroom."
"When will the hospice nurse get here? I want to talk to her."
"I just want to go home, but my mom still wants everything done for me. What should I do?"
"I want to die at home, not here in the hospital."
"I want to be DNR, but don't tell my mother. It will upset her."
"Will the hydromorphone take away all her pain?"
"Why hasn't any lab work been done?"
"We don't want to see the hospice nurse. We're not giving up on her!"
"Laura doesn't need to complete the advanced directives. I still want everything possible done for her."

facilitatorQuestions: Does Laura need oxygen administration? Why or why not?
Explain the difference between hydromorphone IV, oxycodone ER and Fentanyl patch?
How will the dexamethasone help Laura? (Answer: It will help reduce ICP, nausea and bone pain.)
What medications should be administered at this time? Why?
How will you manage Laura's constipation?
How will you manage Laura's nausea?
Who should make the decisions about hospice care and advanced directives?
What should you do when family member's wishes contradict patient wishes?

tabContentChanges.content: Full History & Physical from Dr. Bennett available.
New admission orders from Dr. Bennett available.
Home medications plus hydromorphone and dexamethasone available.
Shows a copy of the completed advance directive form (Appendix B).
Scenario objectives have been met. Are you sure you want to exit the game?

questions.text: How did you feel this scenario went?
Review understanding of learning objective: Communicate effectively and compassionately with the patient, family, and health care team members about end-of-life issues.
subQuestions: What therapeutic techniques did you utilize today? Were they effective?
If you could "do over," would you say anything differently to Laura or her mom?

questions.text: Review understanding of learning objective: Recognize one's own attitudes, feelings, values, and expectations about death and the individual, cultural, and spiritual diversity existing in these beliefs and customs.
subQuestions: What did you learn about your own attitudes, feelings, values and expectation about death while participating in this scenario?

questions.text: Review understanding of learning objective: Demonstrate respect for the patient's views and wishes during end-of-life care.
subQuestions: Whose decisions should be followed regarding Laura's care?
How did you advocate for Laura's wishes about her end of life care?

questions.text: Review understanding of learning objective: Assess symptoms (e.g., pain, dyspnea, constipation, anxiety, fatigue, nausea/vomiting, skin breakdown and altered cognition) commonly experienced by patients at the end of life and intervene appropriately according to evidence based palliative care practices.
subQuestions: Pain: Explain how you performed a focused pain assessment on Laura. Do you believe her pain is well managed? Why or why not? How will hydromorphone IV and dexamethasone PO improve Laura's pain management?
Respiratory status: What was Laura's respiratory status? How did you address it?
GI status: How did you assess Laura's GI status? How does her GI status relate to her overall condition and treatments?

Anxiety/Fear/Depression/Cognitive status: What was Laura's psychosocial status? What stages of grief are Laura and her mom demonstrating today? Do you think Laura is demonstrating any signs of depression? Delirium? Explain?

Skin integrity: What are Laura's risk factors for skin breakdown? What number do you calculate using the Braden scale and what level of risk does this indicate? Did you find any areas of skin breakdown? How would you describe her sacral area? What interventions could be implemented to prevent further skin breakdown?

questions.text: Review understanding of learning objective: Apply legal and ethical principles in end-of-life care, recognizing the influence of personal values, professional codes, and patient preferences.
subQuestions: Compare palliative care/hospice services.
Compare what is contained in a "DNR," "Living Will" and "Power of Attorney for Health Care."
What are the goals for end of life care? Are these goals currently being met for Laura?

questions.text: Review understanding of learning objective: Address spiritual health during end-of-life care
subQuestions: What spiritual cues did you notice when interacting with Laura and her mom?
How could spiritual wellness be incorporated into end of life care for Laura and Jane?

questions.text: Tie the scenario back to the nursing process in a large group discussion. Concept mapping can be used to facilitate discussion.
subQuestions: Identify priority nursing problems you identified for Laura.
Create a patient centered goal for each nursing problem you identified.
Discuss potential focused assessments for each nursing problem.
Discuss priority nursing interventions for each nursing diagnosis.
Re-evaluate the simulation in terms of the nursing process; what was actually accomplished? What could be improved in the future?

"Today you cared for a patient with end stage lung cancer who arrived in the ED with poorly managed pain. You addressed several end of life issues such as pain; dyspnea; advance directives; and an ethical dilemma when the patient's wishes are different from family's wishes. What is one thing you learned from participating in this scenario that you will take with you into your nursing practice?" (Each student must share something different from what the others share.)

debrief.facilitatorNotes: Debriefing technique is based on INACSL Standards for Debriefing and NLN Theory-Based Debriefing by Dreifuerst.
